newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURES - Romanian industry fears painful but needed reform.
newsitem.headline: FEATURES - Romanian industry fears painful but needed reform.

text.p: "We are the one-eyed man in the country of the blind. We produce and we can sell what we produce," says Vasile Scarlat, a manager at Electroputere, a heavy electrical equipment manufacturer.

Six years after Romania's anti-communist revolt and six weeks before its third democratic elections, Electroputere is an exception -- a large industrial firm that operates at a small profit and does not suck vast subsidies from the state.
Across the rest of Romania's grim industrial landscape the picture is different -- armies of workers are employed producing goods nobody wants.
The Balkan country's finances are faltering fast as it dithers over how to dismantle its planned economy, inherited from the communists, while minimising the social cost.

Once Eastern Europe's biggest producer of electric locomotives, Electroputere's plant in Craiova, 250 km (155 miles) southwest of Bucharest, has not been spared the hardships plaguing most of the country's industry.
It suffers from a shortage of orders, crippling financial bottlenecks and a lack of funds for new technology. Its workforce has been halved to 7,500, mostly by natural wastage.
"In 1989, we produced 180 locomotives, mostly for export. This year we produced none," said Scarlat.
Electroputere, a holding of seven production units spread over 80 hectares (198 acres), also produces electric motors, generators, power transformers, and equipment for the transport sector.
The company has scored unusual export success, winning a contract with Germany's Adtranz to build mechanical parts for large locomotives.

"We work at 60 percent capacity but export 40 percent of that output. Without exports we would have long since closed," Scarlat said, pointing to a dimly-lit workshop the size of a soccer field where dozens of workers toiled over machinery.
Scarlat said huge debts owed to the company were to blame for the failure to upgrade equipment, some of it 25 years old.
"Our main problem is not a thin order book but financial blockages which prevent us from investing," Scarlat said.
Post-communist authorities have let arrears grow to a staggering 18 trillion lei ($570 million), almost equal to the country's entire money supply, stifling enterprise with debt.
Nor does the government show any sign of cutting the vast amounts of the budget it throws at inefficient state industries to keep unemployment down to a rosy seven percent.
After the election economists say a foreign debt squeeze and a currency collapse may force tougher action to reform the industrial sector, now 80 percent of gross domestic product.

Small private businesses have flourished since 1989 but the umbrellas of the tiny shops and restaurants, with their Western cigarette and soft drink labels, offer little protection from dark clouds gathering above massive money wasting industry.
"Fine. Let's close down the plants and send everybody home. And what's next?," said a government official.
"It's easy to turn an aquarium into fish soup, but no one knows how to turn fish soup into an aquarium," he added, underlining the lack of a clear-cut strategy for the future.

Refusal to restructure means goods pile up at plants, with some 73 percent of June's industrial production reckoned to have gone straight into storage. The figure has stayed above 60 percent since 1989, official data shows.

The radical surgery recommended for industry by Western advisers would result in a sharp increase in blue-collar unemployment, an unaffordable electoral cost for the leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) government.

Opposition parties like the Democratic Convention and ex-premier Petre Roman's Union of Social Democrats are more market orientated but have shied from prescribing harsh economic medicine for fear of alienating voters ahead of polls.
Some economists say restructuring has been delayed by resistance from communist-era managers who feel their power and perks are threatened.

Privatisation -- so important in other central and Eastern european countries for boosting the economy -- has proceeded slowly, due mainly to domestic capital shortages, thin interest among foreign investors and lukewarm government support.
Many managers, appointed for their loyalty to the PDSR rather than for their talents, are using the absence of a restructuring plan to strip companies of assets, analysts say.
Managers sell state company products at low prices to private firms they or their relatives run and buy raw materials or equipment at high prices from the same outfits.
Many visiting Western executives have complained that corruption, poor infrastructure and confusing property ownership laws have dissuaded them from investing.
Romania is trailing well behind other countries in the region with a mere $1.8 billion in foreign funding since 1989 mainly the beer, soft drink, tobacco and vehicle markets.
A few industrial giants such as Shell, McDonald's Procter & Gamble and Korea's Daewoo have ventured into Romania, hoping to gain a footing that will pay dividends in the future.
